big: Two REITs both show a 7% distribution yield. One has offices 95% let on long leases. The other has 70% let on leases ending soon. The same yield, a very different risk. How do you tell? Four numbers.

lines: Is a higher yield always better?
No. Yield is the payout divided by today's price. It is not a guarantee. Look at occupancy, WALE, NAV and debt too. They show how safe that payout may be.

note: Also check how much debt there is and when loans must be refinanced. Figures are made up.

title: Reading a REIT
stops: A longer WALE makes income less predictable
Yield is a rate on today's unit price
Units always trade at exactly NAV
caps: Units can trade above or below NAV.

q: A REIT pays ₹8 a year on a unit priced at ₹100. What is the distribution yield?
why: 80% would need a payout of ₹80 a unit.
8 ÷ 100 is 8%, the payout over the price.
0.8% would be a payout of only ₹0.80.
100% would need a payout of ₹100 a unit.

q: What does a longer WALE suggest?
opts: Rent will rise sharply next year
The REIT has no debt at all
The unit price must rise soon
why: WALE does not forecast rent rises. The details here point elsewhere.
WALE says nothing about debt. That does not match this case.
WALE does not set the unit price. It does not fit the facts given.
WALE shows how long tenants are committed to stay.

q: A unit trades at ₹100 and the NAV is ₹110. What does that mean?
why: The price is below, not above, NAV.

q: Besides the yield, what else should be checked?
opts: The colour of the REIT's logo
The name of the sponsor's chef
why: A logo says nothing about payouts. It does not answer what was asked.
A chef's name is not relevant. It does not answer what was asked.
Debt and refinancing dates affect payout safety.
A slogan is not data. That does not match this case.

pts: Occupancy shows how much space is let out.
WALE shows how long tenants are committed.
Yield is payout ÷ price. It is not a guarantee. Check NAV and debt.
